It doesn’t feel like a worry; it feels like a fact, like everything is already rotting from the inside and we’re all just waiting for the final crash. I catch myself telling my wife to stop making plans because there’s no point.

Around the same time, I started hearing voices at work. It’s not the animals—these are clear human voices, like two or three people talking just behind me, commenting on what I’m doing, saying things like “pointless” or “why bother.” Sometimes they’re arguing with each other about me. There’s nobody there when I look.

My coworkers say I sometimes make weird faces while I’m cleaning the enclosures, like I’m grimacing or wincing for no reason—I don’t even notice I’m doing it. I did have that bad mauling incident a couple of years ago, but these things I’m describing don’t feel tied to that; they’re more like they came out of nowhere and just took over my life.
D005-D018_h022.question_b:
I work nights at the zoo, mostly with the big cats. About six months ago, a jaguar got out during a storm. It pinned me against the fence before we got it back in. I thought I was going to die. Since then, I’ve been on edge, jumpy at every sound, and I avoid that enclosure if I can. I barely sleep, and when I do, I have the same nightmare of its face right in mine.

The last three months have been worse. Sometimes, especially when I’m near that area or hear metal clanging, it feels like I’m back there. It’s not just a memory—I see it, smell it, hear it, like the whole attack is happening again. In those moments, I hear this voice telling me the world’s about to end, that something terrible is coming because of what happened that night. Even at home, I sometimes catch myself making these weird faces my wife asks about—I only notice when she points it out. The voices and this certainty that everything is going to be destroyed only ever come when I’m triggered by something that reminds me of that night.

I also keep smelling smoke and dead animals when there’s nothing there. I’ll stop in the middle of a fire road, searching for a campfire or a carcass, and there’s absolutely nothing. It’s strong enough that I almost gag sometimes.

I get really wound up and restless. I can’t sit still in the cabin—pacing, checking the windows, going in and out even when there’s no call, no storm, nothing going on.
